entities.name: Quintus Fabius Maximus Sanga
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Quintus Fabius Maximus Sanga, a prominent figure of the late Roman Republic, was appointed suffect consul by Julius Caesar in 45 BCE, a critical year that underscored the dictator's near-absolute control over Roman political life. A scion of the illustrious Fabia gens, his brief tenure in the highest office reflected the dramatic shifts in governance occurring as the Republic transitioned into the Principate. His life and career are intimately tied to the tumultuous period of the Roman Civil Wars and the consolidation of Caesar's power, marking him as a participant in the twilight of republican institutions.

Fabius Maximus's political ascent was primarily facilitated by his staunch allegiance to Julius Caesar during the Roman Civil Wars. He served as a legate under Caesar, participating in the decisive campaign in Hispania against the Pompeian forces, culminating in the Battle of Munda in 45 BCE. Following this victory, Caesar returned to Rome and, in a demonstration of his unchallenged authority, appointed Fabius Maximus to the consulship, replacing Gaius Caninius Rebilus, who had himself served only a single day. Fabius Maximus assumed office on the Kalends of October (October 1st) 45 BCE, sharing the position with Gaius Trebonius.

The swift succession of consuls, with Fabius Maximus's appointment and his subsequent unexpected death on December 31st, 45 BCE, further highlighted the erosion of traditional republican norms under Caesar. His death led to another rapid appointment, with Gaius Caninius Rebilus again serving a single day on the very last day of the year, a situation that became a source of historical anecdote and satire regarding the trivialization of the consulship. Fabius Maximus's career, though brief in its highest office, thus serves as a vivid illustration of the political landscape shaped by Caesar's dictatorial rule and the profound instability preceding the Republic's final collapse.
